annotations.keyFindings: A staggered nurse-driven removal protocol across 9 hospitals was followed by a fall from 21 to 14 catheter days per 100 patient days, with level changes in 7 of 9 hospitals; infection rates changed unclearly (2.1 and 1.9 per 1,000 catheter days).
annotations.limitations: Non-randomised staggered design; infections too few for precision.

annotations.keyFindings: Mapping 40 patients showed a median wait of 2.5 days between a catheter no longer being needed and its removal, mostly at handoffs; after standard work the wait fell to 1 day.
annotations.limitations: One hospital; no comparison group; small samples.

annotations.keyFindings: Across 31 studies catheter use fell by a median of 32 percent; in 8 studies with enough events the pooled infection rate ratio was 0.69 with high heterogeneity; time-series studies reported smaller effects.
annotations.limitations: Mostly uncontrolled before-and-after studies at high risk of bias.

annotations.keyFindings: Twice-weekly point counts estimated monthly catheter days within 8 percent of flowsheet values; mixing sources within one ward's series is discouraged.
annotations.limitations: Fourteen wards; short catheterisations missed by counts.

annotations.keyFindings: In simulations with four sites and three-month intervals, staggered starts detected a 25 percent level change with 80 percent power against 55 percent for simultaneous starts.
annotations.limitations: Simulation-based methods paper; assumptions about autocorrelation.

annotations.keyFindings: Reinsertion within 72 hours followed 5.2 percent of 1,240 nurse-driven removals, mostly retention in older men after surgery.
Nurses were unsure whether they could remove catheters without an order, feared reinsertion, and lost indications at handoffs; written protocols were linked to fewer delays.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Nurse-driven removal with daily review is consistently followed by fewer catheter days (21 to 14 per 100 patient days across 9 hospitals), while infection effects are imprecise and larger in weaker designs. Value stream mapping located most removal delay at handoffs. A staggered start across four sites gives far more power than a simultaneous start. Point counts can measure catheter days on paper-record wards if the source is not mixed within a series. Reinsertion after removal is about 5 percent and should be tracked. Nurses need explicit authority to remove catheters.
gradeRationale: Time-series and before-and-after studies with consistent reductions in catheter use but imprecise and heterogeneous infection effects; a simulation-based methods paper and small qualitative work.
summary: Seven records appraised; six source-derived claims; overall certainty low.
